items.title: A New Transformer for TEMPORAL Attention #ai
items.summary: A new temporal causal reasoning former (TCR-Former) with a modified temporal attention mechanism. Note: One of the new elements is a separate "event slot", or multiples of them (128). An event slot is a learned numerical representation of a potential event from the text itself, not the event itself, not a timestamp alone, and not a causal rule. Its sole purpose is to gather event information into a form that can be temporally supervised and supplied to the decoder. Another way to see it is that each event slot is kind of an additional feature vector for temporal causal reasoning. Its intended purpose is to collect information about one potential event from the document and provide that information to the reasoning decoder. The earlier "event slots" cannot directly read the later slots. This is the intended connection between the ordered slots and temporal reasoning: later event representations can build on earlier representations. The linear sequence of those event slots provides an ordered scaffold for temporal representations. The authors intend the model to learn a correspondence between position in the event-slot sequence and the temporal organization of events. That ordering is an important part That ordering is an important part, but the main "temporal learning" is happening on the complex encoder-projector-decoder system. The model receives ordered event–timestamp supervision, and the "timestamp head" (see video) encourages slot representations to predict (!) the associated event times. So we have: ordered event slots + directional attention + temporal supervision. all rights w/ authors: From Document Layout to Causal Topology: An End-to-End Architecture for Temporal Causal Reasoning Zhifeng Yang1, Wei Luo1, Yongjian Chen1, Shiqi Ou1,2† from 1 School of Future Technology, South China University of Technology 2 Guangdong Artificial Intelligence and Digital Economy Laboratory (Guangzhou) #airesearch #ainnovation #aitech

items.title: Text-to-speech prompting tips
items.summary: How to prompt a text-to-speech model for voice agents: hyphens for stutters, ellipses for pauses, capitals and punctuation for emphasis, and how AssemblyAI TTS reads currency, email addresses, dates, abbreviations and phone numbers. Every tip is tested live in the AssemblyAI playground. The full prompting guide, as a markdown file you can hand to your agent: https://www.assemblyai.com/docs/tts/prompting-guide.md?utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=tts-prompting-tips&utm_source=youtube Try our API for free → https://www.assemblyai.com/dashboard/signup?utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=tts-prompting-tips&utm_source=youtube Pacing and tone come from how you write the text. Hyphens make a voice stutter over a word, three dots add a pause (where you put them matters), and capitals, exclamation marks and questions change what the voice emphasizes and how a sentence ends. Filler words are written out, and two letters are enough: "hm" comes out as "hmm". A word followed by a hyphen and a space gives you a false start. Voice agents spend most of their time reading out numbers, addresses and confirmation codes, so the second half covers normalization: a dollar sign makes an amount read as dollars, email addresses are read out as addresses, a date written in numbers is read month first (even 24/10/2026 came out as October 24th), "St" is read as "Street", and common abbreviations like USA and MIT are read as expected. For a less common acronym, put hyphens between the letters. And for numbers, hyphens group the digits, while a comma makes "4,321" read as a whole number. items.title: L&T's massive 52 MW AI data centre is coming to Chennai
